knowledge_graph.title: Border disease
knowledge_graph.description: Border disease is a viral disease of sheep and goats, primarily causing congenital diseases, but can also cause acute and persistent infections. It first appeared in the border regions of England and Wales in 1959, and has since spread world-wide.

related_questions.question: What causes border disease?
related_questions.snippet: BD is caused by the Pestivirus border disease virus (BDV), but in some parts of the world, especially where there is close contact between sheep or goats and cattle, the same clinical signs may be caused by infection with bovine viral diarrhoea virus (BVDV).

related_questions.question: What is another name for border disease?
related_questions.snippet: Border disease exists worldwide in sheep, and also is known regionally as “hairy shaker disease” or “fuzzy lamb syndrome.” Border disease-like viruses have been isolated from nondomestic sheep and goats, suggesting the possibility of wildlife reservoirs for this virus.

related_questions.question: Is border disease in the US?
related_questions.snippet: The disease has been recognized in most sheep-rearing areas of the world, including the western USA. Surviving lambs are persistently infected with border disease virus, and no effective treatment is known.

text_blocks.snippet: Border disease (BD) is a viral disease primarily affecting sheep and goats, caused by the Border disease virus (BDV), a pestivirus. It was first identified in 1959 in the border region between England and Wales. The virus can lead to infertility, abortions, and the birth of "hairy shaker" lambs, which exhibit tremors and abnormal wool growth.
snippet_highlighted_words: a viral disease primarily affecting sheep and goats, caused by the Border disease virus (BDV), a pestivirus

list.title: Etiology:
list.snippet: BDV, a pestivirus, is the causative agent, closely related to bovine viral diarrhea virus (BVDV) and classical swine fever virus (CSFV).

list.title: Transmission:
list.snippet: BDV primarily spreads through the placenta from infected ewes to lambs. Persistently infected (PI) animals, those infected in utero, are the main source of virus spread.
In sheep: Barren ewes, abortions, stillbirths, and the birth of small, weak lambs with tremors (hairy shaker lambs) are common.
In goats: Similar to sheep, but hair coat changes are rare.
In cattle: While not a primary host, cattle can be affected, and BDV can complicate BVDV eradication efforts.

list.title: Economic impact:
list.snippet: BDV can cause significant economic losses due to reduced lambing rates, increased mortality, and the need for control measures.

list.title: Diagnosis:
list.snippet: Diagnosis involves identifying BDV-specific antibodies or antigens in affected animals.
Maintaining a closed flock: Minimizing the introduction of new animals can help prevent the introduction of BDV.
Testing and isolation: Blood testing and isolating new additions can help identify and manage infected animals.
Vaccination: While a commercial BDV vaccine exists, its effectiveness can be limited due to antigenic diversity among BDV strains.
Biosecurity measures: Implementing measures to prevent contact between sheep, goats, and cattle can help control the spread of the virus.
